title: I'm using Pixel Lab. Are there any alternatives that are as good?
author: AsparagusOk8818
selftext:
...I really appreciate the extraordinarily high quality and robust features of Pixel Lab. 

But it is very, very expensive, IMHO. And I'm not complaining about the price, it is plainly worth the price tag - but I do not know if I can afford to use it. x.x 

I don't suppose someone knows of a cheaper option?

comments.author: nykwil
comments.body: I can't imagine anything under 10-12 dollars a month. You can run stuff locally?

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
Well... how to put this: 

Pixel Lab's most basic plan is for 2,000 generations/month. And that sounds okay, except that when they say '2,000 generations', they actually just mean 2,000 abstract tokens that you must spend 20 at a time for a good generation. 

So, 100 images per month. 

But less than that because every edit is also a generation. 

  
So you have to at a minimum take the next plan up at $24 USD/month. 

And this is 5,000 credit per month, at 20 credit per generation. 250 generations/month

  
It's just... not a lot.

comments.author: SlashForward
comments.body: I'm in the same boat, I think the best bang for buck Pixel Lab is up there. The only alternative that I have found is to just do it locally, easier said than done though.

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
All of the local options I have explored are complete ass. Just utterly useless crap. 

I found this, though: 

[Pixel Art Generator - Sprite Fusion](https://www.spritefusion.com/pixel-art-generator/editor)

Is it cheaper? No. The cheapest option right now is to generate 'pixel' art via GPT and then run it through a pixel grid fixer. The problem with that method is that there's just no way to control your sprite resolution. 

But the posted option is sure really cool, and does all of the things I wish Pixel Lab would be more focused on a lot better (and the training data is plainly much more specific if less robust than Pixel Labs's training data).

replies.author: whoji
replies.body: Wonder if you have found any better solutions?

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
Unfortunately I have not, and I spent a week going down a rabbit hole of possible options.

Sprite Fusion is the best quality option I could find, and it is too expensive for me.

  
All of the local options via ComfyUI are unacceptable. I have tried every single LoRA that would work for every single image generator that will fit in my admittedly tiny 6GB of VRAM, and even went ahead and installed a few models that began pagefiling my SSD.

They could not produce even 1 single usable sprite. It was all complete garbage.

  
What I'm doing right now, that only really works because it matches the aesthetic of my current game, is this: 

 \- Generate a Sumi-E ink style painting of the thing I want using ChatGPT - typically telling it to generate 4 variations on a 2x2 grid of squares, so I can pick the best output from that. Very few rerolls needed that way.   
 \- Take the image I want into [Pixel Rabbit — Free Image & GIF to Pixel Art Converter](https://portalrabbit.com/) , set it to Grid Artist, and I use the 192 px long edge and 32 colors. Output the pixel art from the image.  
 \- Take the image into GIMP and apply scanline distortions to it and put a color flattening filter over it.

That last step is obviously not necessary if you don't deliberately want images that look like they were rendered on an old monitor in-game, and Sumi-E Ink style won't be appropriate if you want a traditional sprite character on a transparent background. But the same process can and does work if you tell GPT to output characters on a transparent background.

The thing to be conscious of is the amount of clean-up work you'll have to manually do if you want transparent sprite characters via GPT. The outlines will be a mess - so you have to go in and manually cut them down to a 1 pixel width fit.

And DO NOT tell GPT to output a pixel art character. Tell it to do some other kind of style, or you will have huge problems with scaling, because GPT never uses a consistent value for it's psuedo-pixels. Tell it to do vector art (don't worry, it won't actually draw vector art. For whatever reason it interprets 'vector art' as just meaning a very high fidelity traditional raster art sprite).
